title: Displaying data

match.reason: No point in the bank teaches how to draw and choose data displays; the closest, types of data, only covers working out the data type before a display is chosen.

draft.title: Displaying data
card: uses separate bars with gaps between them. It suits categorical data, such as the favourite sport of each student in a class.
puts one dot above a number on a number line for each score. It suits small sets of numerical data, such as 12 test marks out of 10.
uses touching bars, each covering a class interval, such as 0 to 9 or 10 to 19. It suits large sets of numerical data, especially measures.
splits each value into a stem and a leaf, so 47 has stem 4 and leaf 7. It shows the shape and keeps every original value.
draft.remember: Gaps between bars suit categories. Touching bars suit grouped numbers.

a.q: Which display suits the data on the favourite pet of each student in a class?
a.why: Favourite pet is categorical, so separate bars with gaps suit it. A histogram is for grouped numerical data, and it has touching bars.
a.clue: Pets are names of groups, not numbers.

b.q: Dev records the exact height of each of 200 students and wants to group the heights in intervals. Which display suits this best?
b.why: Heights are numerical and there are many of them, so grouping them in class intervals with a histogram suits. A dot plot suits small sets, and a column graph suits categories.
b.clue: Think of a large set of measures grouped in intervals.

check.summary: No problems found. The card's descriptions of the four displays are accurate, and both questions have one clearly right answer that matches the writer's explanations.
